claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 undergoes complex phase transformations whose crystallization temperatures depend on cooling rate.
The alloy exhibits extensive formation of several primary non-eutectic crystalline phases.
Rapidly quenched Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is initially amorphous or partially amorphous.
Slower cooling or subsequent reheating causes extensive primary crystallization in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
A 0.5-second flash anneal at approximately 825–860 K is 10–15% below a crystallization onset of approximately 960 K.
The proposed 825–860 K annealing interval is below the glass-transition temperature.
A relevant slower-cooling boundary is approximately 52 K/s.
Flash annealing immediately after quenching will relax the atomic configuration, reduce excess free volume, and minimize internal stresses.
Reduced free volume and internal stress will produce fewer nucleation sites for crystalline phases.
The short anneal permits structural relaxation without allowing enough time for crystalline ordering.
Structural relaxation reduces the kinetic driving force for nucleation and consequently delays or suppresses primary crystallization during later thermal cycles.
Flash-annealed samples will retain a higher amorphous fraction than untreated, as-quenched samples.
Flash-annealed samples will exhibit a higher DSC crystallization-onset temperature than untreated samples.
Flash annealing will reduce the multiple exothermic DSC peaks associated with crystallization.
Amorphous melt-spun ribbon can show a glass transition followed by two crystallization exotherms during reheating.
Higher annealing temperatures or longer dwell times could initiate unwanted crystallization, whereas lower temperatures might provide insufficient relaxation.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant greater-than-10% increase in crystallization-onset temperature together with reduced crystalline-phase formation would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The proposed temperature is defined as 10–15% below the crystallization onset, but repeatedly called 'sub-Tg.' Being below Tx does not establish that it is below Tg, and no same-system Tg is supplied. The cited amorphous-alloy record instead reports Tg = 623.6 ± 9.1 K and Tx = 731.8 ± 3.1 K, which would make 825–860 K neither sub-Tg nor sub-Tx if those values were applicable.

The intervention is applied only after solidification, yet it is claimed to be effective across slower-cooling conditions. A post-solidification anneal cannot suppress primary phases that have already formed during the preceding slow-cooling trajectory; the hypothesis would need to distinguish prevention during cooling from stability during later reheating.
